title: Reconciliation
hook: the sacrament of return, where sins are forgiven through a priest (CCC 1422)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist, source and summit. Your line was everything flows from the table. Did you pause and give thanks at a meal? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

There's a story Jesus tells about a son who takes his inheritance early, leaves home, and spends it all. He ends up feeding pigs and wishing he could eat what they eat. So he rehearses a speech, and starts the long walk home. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." The son never gets to the end of his speech. Catholics say there's a sacrament built on that run. Today: reconciliation.
screen: `A SON WHO SPENT IT ALL.` → `THE LONG WALK HOME.` → `THE FATHER RUNS.`

segments.voice: This sacrament has several names, and each one shows a side of it. Confession, because you say out loud what you've done. Penance, because you turn around and begin to make amends. And reconciliation, because the point is being brought back together. The Latin reconciliare means to bring together again, to restore. Catholics believe it's the ordinary way God forgives serious sins committed after baptism. Where does it come from? In John's Gospel, on the evening of the resurrection, Jesus breathes on the apostles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained." The Catholic Church reads that as Jesus handing on the power to forgive, which is why a priest hears confession. A natural question is: why tell a person? Why not just tell God? Catholics answer in a few ways. Sin isn't only private; it hurts a whole body of people, so the return has a human face too. Saying it aloud makes it real, and hearing the words of forgiveness aloud makes that real as well. And the priest, they believe, acts in the person of Christ, so it's God who forgives. Catholics are asked to go at least once a year if they've committed a serious sin, and some go far more often. Other Christians do this differently: the Orthodox also confess to a priest; Anglicans and Lutherans offer private confession without requiring it; other Protestants confess to God directly and to one another. Tomorrow's sacrament heals too, in a different way.
screen: `CONFESSION, PENANCE, RECONCILIATION.` · `RECONCILIARE: TO BRING BACK TOGETHER.` · `WHOSE SINS YOU SHALL FORGIVE.` · `WHY SAY IT TO A PERSON?` · then, large: `THE FATHER RUNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the road home. Settle, and breathe. Picture the son on the road, going over his speech one more time. Then picture the figure far off at the end of it, already running. If there's something you've been rehearsing an apology for, let it come to mind. Don't polish the speech. Just let it be what it is. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God as it is. If you don't, just stay with the picture of being met halfway. The bell holds the time.
Reconciliation. From the Latin for bringing back together. The sacrament of return, where Catholics confess to a priest and hear that they're forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: there's always a way back. Today, take one small step toward someone you're at odds with. A message, a smile, a hello. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics go to confession by speaking their sins to a priest, in a confessional or face to face, and receive absolution; many parishes offer it on Saturday afternoons and especially in Advent and Lent.

notes: Names of the sacrament: CCC 1423–1424 lists conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness, reconciliation. Three used. Confirm.
Annual confession of grave sins: canon 989 / CCC 1457. Confirm phrasing 'if they've committed a serious sin'.
'in the person of Christ' (in persona Christi). Confirm simplification.
Other churches summarized briefly (Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant). Confirm fairness.
Etymology of reconciliare ('bring into council') is a common gloss; conciliare = to bring together, win over. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed a garbled hook sentence ('And the father, ... his father saw him'); 'doesn't let the son finish' softened (Luke 15:21 has him say part of it); reconciliare now glossed 'bring together again, restore' instead of the preacher's 'bring back into council'; 'ordinary way' limited to serious sins (CCC 1497); 'many go far more often' and 'most Protestants' replaced; practice reworked so it no longer repeats day 105's 'one thing you wish you hadn't done'.
